content: Hepatitis A, previously referred to as infectious hepatitis or epidemical virus, is an acute liver disease caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV), an RNA virus. The primary mode of transmission is fecal-oral, occurring through the ingestion of contaminated food or water or direct contact with an infected individual. Globally, tens of millions of people are estimated to contract hepatitis A annually. In regions with poor hygiene and sanitation, particularly in developing countries, hepatitis A infection is highly prevalent and often acquired during early childhood. In these cases, over 90% of infected children remain asymptomatic, and the infection provides lifelong immunity, making it less clinically significant. However, in industrialized nations such as the United States and Europe, the infection is more commonly seen in susceptible young adults, often contracted during travel to endemic areas or through contact with infected individuals. The hepatitis A virus was first identified in 1973 and was distinguished from other forms of hepatitis during World War II. Its transmission routes and prevalence were better understood later. In 1995-1996, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved inactivated hepatitis A vaccines, transforming the disease into a vaccine-preventable condition. Hepatitis A primarily affects the liver. The virus is most infectious approximately two weeks before the onset of jaundice. Gross examination of the liver in affected individuals may reveal an enlarged, erythematous organ, while microscopic analysis shows lymphocyte infiltration and inflammation of the portal tracts. The differential diagnosis of hepatitis A includes other conditions that present with fever, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, icteric sclera, and elevated liver enzymes (ALT and AST). These conditions include other viral hepatitis types, alcoholic hepatitis, and autoimmune hepatitis. The epidemiology of hepatitis A varies significantly across different regions and time periods. Historically, the disease was more prevalent in children, but in recent years, it has become more common in adults. In the United States, the incidence in 2011 was 0.4 cases per 100,000 population. The introduction of the hepatitis A vaccine has reduced disparities in infection rates among racial and ethnic groups and has minimized geographic differences in incidence in developed countries. In contrast, in developing nations with poor sanitation, up to 90% of children are infected with HAV by the age of 10. Individuals at higher risk of contracting hepatitis A include those who are unvaccinated and travel to endemic areas with inadequate sanitation and unsafe water. Other risk factors include intravenous drug use, living with an infected person, having a sexual partner with acute HAV infection, and attending childcare centers. Screening for hepatitis A involves detecting HAV antibodies in the blood. Anti-HAV IgG remains elevated after acute infection and indicates immunity. Hepatitis A is generally a self-limiting disease with an incubation period of approximately 28 days. While children often experience asymptomatic or mild infections, over 80% of adults develop symptoms such as fatigue, malaise, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. Complications, though rare, may include dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, bleeding, and fulminant hepatitis. Prognosis depends on the patient’s age and underlying liver health. Approximately 10-15% of patients may experience a relapse of symptoms within six months of the acute illness. The clinical presentation of hepatitis A can range from asymptomatic to symptomatic. Common symptoms include fever, fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and jaundice. Physical examination findings may include fever, jaundice, icteric sclera, abdominal tenderness, and hepatomegaly. Other findings may include rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, abdominal distension, ascites, and altered mental status. Laboratory diagnosis of hepatitis A requires serologic testing. The presence of IgM anti-HAV during the acute phase is the gold standard for diagnosis, while IgG anti-HAV remains elevated for life, indicating past infection or immunity. Additional findings may include elevated direct bilirubin and liver enzymes. Detection of HAV RNA through sequencing can also confirm the diagnosis. Liver biopsy is rarely needed and is reserved for unclear cases or suspected relapses. Imaging studies, such as CT scans, are not typically used for diagnosing hepatitis A but may be performed to rule out other conditions. Abdominal ultrasound may be used to exclude other causes of hepatomegaly or chronic liver disease. Common ultrasound findings in acute hepatitis A include increased brightness of the portal vein walls and decreased liver echogenicity. There is no specific antiviral treatment for hepatitis A. Management focuses on supportive care, including maintaining hydration and nutritional balance. Recovery may take several weeks to months. In cases of fulminant hepatitis, aggressive supportive therapy and potential liver transplantation may be required. Primary prevention of hepatitis A involves vaccination and the use of immune globulin (IG). The hepatitis A vaccine is administered intramuscularly in a two-dose series, with doses given at 0 and 6-12 months. The vaccine induces protective antibody levels in nearly all adults, with 94-100% achieving protection after the first dose and 100% after the second dose. Vaccination is the most effective method of preventing HAV transmission, particularly in high-risk groups such as men who have sex with men (MSM), illicit drug users, and individuals with chronic liver disease.
